153.t: Ted Reed's Syncopation, Morris Goldenberg and Ed Straight
153.s: Brief remarks on Reed's Syncopation, Goldenberg's students and Chicago teacher Ed Straight, whom he likened to Roy Knapp.
153.ch: More drummers, teachers and advice for students
153.q: That’s a good book. Ted’s a good teacher too. I got to know him quite well. Even when he moved on from New York to Florida, I’d see him quite often. Good. Nice man.

153.t: Gene Krupa's rudiments book and The Mighty Two video
153.s: Bellson recalls arranging the 26 rudiments to swing time for their video The Mighty Two, and doubts Krupa wrote his book himself.
153.q: Yes I am. Gene was another example of a guy that didn’t read too much. I didn’t know that. I thought he was well schooled, even though he studied something with Roy Knapp, but he had problems with reading too. In fact we made a video and a book called The Mighty Two. You know about that one? It’s…

153.t: Their Time Was the Greatest: play-along book honoring 12 drummers
153.s: His publication lets students play charts with a band while he plays in the style of Rich, Webb, Catlett, Jo Jones, Roach, Gadd and others.
153.q: This has worked out real good, because it gives the drummer a chance to look at a chart and play it – put the headset on and play it with the band. They muffle my part way down, but not completely out. The drummer can play the chart and hear me a little bit, enough to realize what I did, how I…

153.s: Dawson performed all rudiments with brushes over a samba bass-drum pattern at clinics and taught Tony Williams.
153.ch: More drummers, teachers and advice for students
153.q: Alan, a champion. A champion all the way. Beautiful drummer. He did something I’ve never seen anybody ever do, at a clinic. Picks a set of brushes and goes through all the rudiments, playing brushes, while he’s playing a samba beat with the bass drum, da-dum, da-dum, da-dum, da-dum. That’s…

153.t: Writing the reading-text books for all instruments
153.s: Seeing little drum material in his father's store, he wrote hundreds of pages of rhythm exercises that Gil Breines condensed into Modern Reading Texts.
153.q: When I was working for my dad in the music store, I noticed that there wasn’t too much material in those days for drums. It was always, here’s how you hold the left hand, the right hand. They didn’t even talk about matched grip then. It was all conventional grip. So I decided to write some…

153.t: Charlie Wilcoxon and drummer George Steinbrenner
153.s: A great teacher, Wilcoxon kept a large portrait of Bellson in the studio, which his student George Steinbrenner remembered.
153.ch: More drummers, teachers and advice for students
153.q: He was a great teacher. In fact, Charlie Wilcoxson. I’m a Yankee ballplayer fan. I’m a Yankee fan, for years. Pearl used to go up to Yankee Stadium and sing the Star- Spangled Banner. I got to know George Steinbrenner. George Steinbrenner was a drummer when he was younger, and he took lessons from…

493.s: His first drum teacher was James Black, who taught fundamentals from Stick Control. Marsalis jokes that no drummer has gotten past page five.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: My first teacher was a drummer by the name of James Black who I later found out was my father’s partner in crime as far as music goes. At that time, what I learned from James was fundamentals, such as the book, which I later discovered was the bible of drum books, or the J. S. Bach drum books, if…

493.s: Dawson asked if he knew Stick Control and showed how to apply it to the drum set. Marsalis took only one lesson then and a few years later.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: Yeah. When he said that, I said, oh, okay. I said, all right. This is okay, somebody to respect. The first lesson, the one thing that I remembered from that lesson – we had discussed some things here and there, but the one thing I remembered was, is that – was that the great Alan Dawson said, “Yes,…

493.t: Isaac Edgerton in Richmond and learning to read drum music
493.s: In Richmond he studied with VCU student Isaac Edgerton, who introduced him to rudiments and the Ludwig drum solo book. He also recalls Suzuki violin with Janet Newman.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: I have a vague recollection of it, but I do remember the Stick Control. I believe there’s a recording of that lesson that I need to try to find. I need to try to find that. I don’t know if I have it. Delfeayo might have it. I need to try to find that tape and go through that to see what he was…

493.t: Drum method books and timpani study
493.s: They discuss books such as Haskell Harr, Wilcoxon, Saul Goodman and Vic Firth. He played timpani repertoire in orchestras without owning a set.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: No. It’s funny. I have that book. I have Accents and Rebounds. It just didn’t happen. When I studied, it was different books that we had, like Haskell Harr Drum Method. That was one. There was, I think, some of the Goldenberg method books. There was . . .

493.t: Giving up violin and studying classical percussion
493.s: He quit the violin and studied snare and timpani with David DeGroot, Jim Atwood and Leland Beach. By eighth grade he was playing full shows with his father.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: I want to say it was a week, maybe a week and a half. No, I think it was a week, because I seem to remember it was a weekend where I went to do the shoot and did the concert, and then it was like Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. I think it was Friday I said, “Look. I got to get back home, man, because…

493.t: Playing Delfeayo's Berklee recital and being sent to Alan Dawson
493.s: At eight he sat in on his father's shows. Delfeayo then had him write tunes and play his Berklee recital, where he stayed up late at Wally's and learned of the Dawson lesson.
493.ch: First drum teachers and early training
493.q: Six, seven. I’m going to say seven. I would have been too young to understand a lot of that at that time. But it was a lot of fundamentals. A lot of those lessons I don’t remember as well, but it was at that time – but I do remember a lot of the fundamentals. There’s other things that I don’t…

147.t: Teaching himself to read, and the first Broadway musical
147.s: Crawford says he taught himself to read drum books and began studying when he started Broadway musicals, around 1949-50 with Alive and Kicking.
147.ch: Precision, the union and learning to read
147.q: I taught myself. Take a little drink of apple cider, you all. What I'm trying to say is, I taught myself, just like I'm sitting here now, starting at the beginning of a book, when I find I've got enough sense in my head. I got a lot of books here on drums, to sit and practice on. Do it slow, that's…

147.t: Teaching himself drums and learning paradiddles from Cozy Cole
147.s: He had no teacher, learned on the job in Lunceford's band, and later asked Cozy Cole how to play ratamacues and paradiddles.
147.ch: Learning the drums and early influences
147.q: I didn't have no formal education on drums. I didn't have a teacher or nothing. I just sat behind them and just started to banging on them in Lunsford's band.

147.t: Studying rudiments and xylophone after starting the shows
147.s: Crawford began weekly lessons on rudiments on the practice pad and studied xylophone to become a percussionist.
147.q: Yeah, shows. I knew that I had to have something else. I started to studying xylophones to try to become a percussionist, and I got the xylophones up there now. And so I just had to study, for all the pride and everything else behind me.

871.t: Cantrell's method, strictness and Perron band personnel
871.s: Lessons used Carl Fischer's method; Cantrell was strict, sent him to sub in Perron's band, whose members are named, and taught strict time and footwork.
871.q: Light sticks. Light sticks. Do you remember anything else about your lessons? What he did? Did you have a method book or how he taught you? Oh, I have a method book. Fisher's method. Oh, Fisher. Yeah, Fisher. Is that the Otto Lange or Carl Fisher? Carl Fisher. It wasn't the Lange? No. Carl Fisher.…

871.t: Cantrell's lessons: fees, practice, rolls and strictness
871.s: Lessons twice weekly at fifty cents; two hours' practice daily; nine months on the pad before the drum, mostly rolls; Cantrell was strict.
871.q: Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, you see it's different with orchestra than with the little bands that you're affiliated with. Because this is the reason why I say I can play all the folks with any kind of type of drumming because I play with them all. I play with fellas that couldn't read and I play…

798.t: Teacher Dave Perkins and his versatility
798.s: Dave Perkins knew Clark's father and taught and played all instruments. The interviewers ask whether he also played drums.
798.q: Oh, Dave Perkins. He's dead, he's been dead now I guess, oh twenty, oh I guess thirty some odd years. Because he died before my mother did.

798.t: Length of lessons, beating time, and the Langley method book
798.s: Clark studied with Perkins for about a year and ten months until Perkins fell sick. Perkins taught four-four and waltz time by foot, and Clark started on the Langley method.
798.q: Well Mr. Russell I'll tell you. I didn't take lessons very long because he passed. I took lessons I guess about a year and ten months. And he'd taken sick. And when he'd taken sick he couldn't teach anymore. Well I was pretty well going then. Because what he put in this I kept it there. And after…

899.t: Tom-toms, woodblock and details of Cottrell's lessons
899.s: He used a Chinese tom-tom and woodblock, and recalls Cottrell's kindness, the practice pad, 50-cent lessons, and hearing him in brass bands.
899.ch: Learning the drums and first job
899.q: I can tell you he was a very good drummer. And I was interested in what he showed me, you know, what he taught me. And he's a very nice fella to get along with, cause nice disposition, you know. When I'd go to his house, he would greet me with a smile. Yeah.

899.s: He took lessons from strict teacher Louis Cottrell, recommended by his father, but gave up reading; Cottrell played with Perez at the roof garden.
899.ch: Learning the drums and first job
899.q: And I took a few lessons with him and then, I don't know, I just stopped and I liked the jazz. I didn't care too much about reading. I'm sorry I didn't keep it up then.

922.t: Lesson fees and his father's drum pupils
922.s: Lessons cost 25 to 50 cents; pupils included Freddie Coleman, Albert France, Trepagnier; many drummers followed his parades.
922.q: And the last student of his that really turned out to be a real nice drummer was Freddie Coleman. That's the last one. Coleman was his last student that I can remember. Now, another one that was his student, I was a very small boy at the time, it was Albert France. I don't know if you knew Albert…

922.t: How his father learned drums from John Kornfeld and taught the wrist roll
922.s: The father taught himself via a white boyhood friend's lessons and stressed wrist and the roll.
922.q: Oh, yes. He always started them off first, just as he did with me. He started them the same for his, for some. Then after it would be with the pad because he said it would develop a better wrist on a pad than to try him out on a drum. Oh, wow. Because he had exceptional wrist and I must say, by me…

192.t: Learning drums: Doc Bechet, method book and practice
192.s: He learned from Doc Bechet's method, Louis Cottrell and Bush Hall, and practiced alone.
192.q: That was a Carl Fisher. Carl Fisher. Carl Fisher method, that's right. The old drum method. The old Carl Fisher method. The old stuff stuff One who used to give me ideas about different divisions of music was Bush Hall, trumpet player, like I tell you, we played with the Young Tuxedo Band. And he…

192.t: Practicing on tables and the Ted Lewis record
192.s: As a boy he practiced on tables and played along with a Ted Lewis record.
192.q: Never practiced on a drum pad in my life. Never did practice on a drum. I used to practice on a drum. I used to practice on a drum. Tables. I've seen drum pads in later years, you know, at different music stores, but I didn't know what that looked like years ago. Oh, I guess so. It used to take…

378.t: Learning from pit drummers and teaching himself harmony
378.s: On trains and backstage he studies harmony books and practices softly between shows; theater drummers invited him home and taught him.
378.q: But it was a means, I was learning and during that time I WAS TRAVelling on trains -- I was studying harmony, and I taught myself to read, all during this period. I was getting it and I learned so much from drummers in the pit.

378.t: No music for the instrument; owing a debt to the drummers
378.s: There was little music for xylophone except a George Hamilton Green book; he later helps other players because of what the drummers did for him.
378.q: So, I noticed that I could do what I wanted to do on those -- I found that not having any music -- there was no music for that instrument in those days, I had to on -- play like violin books, I'd learned to read out of

103.t: Alan Dawson and finding successors to teach
103.s: Hinton credits Alan Dawson with teaching Jones's sock cymbal and brush work; Jones recalls meeting him in Boston and sending him to a teacher.
103.q: So now we come in the world with nothing; we go out with nothing. Wherever we could catch kids, instead of having a quart of whiskey on one arm and a chick on the other, we went and got these peoples and said, "Come on, it's out here." We couldn't play all 48 states. I said, "Alon, who are you…

103.t: Sol Gubin; learning to tune drums from Jimmy Bertrand and Holland Harold
103.s: Jones says he learned drum tuning from Bertrand and from Holland Harold, an Omaha drummer and teacher.
103.q: Sol is definitely a percussionist... When you say a percussionist, a guy that can play whatever it is and can tune these drums and what have you. I didn't know anything about tuning drums until I got with a saxophone

177.t: How Chaligny taught: snare, counting and keeping time; drumming in the family
177.s: Two years of snare drum with a pad, counting aloud and patting the foot; time must come from within the player. He feels drumming was born in him and sees it in his grandsons.
177.q: Yeah, when we went to lesson, you used a drum pad at lesson, but when the big band was together, well, everybody had the instruments. They would play the instruments.

769.t: A young Indianapolis drummer and learning to read from Paul Barbarin
769.s: He shows a big-band drummer how to make a press roll and recalls brief lessons with Paul Barbarin and Henry Martin.
769.q: And they had a young drummer and he came back behind the curtain and asked him, said, how do you do that? I said, do what? He said, make that roll. Mm-hmm. I said, press roll? He said, that's what they call it? I said, yeah. Mm-hmm. Well, I couldn't understand it. It saved my life. A person playing…

1050.t: Drum teachers: Roy Knapp, Art Layfield and Paul Ash
1050.s: Bertrand lists his teachers, including Roy Knapp and Art Layfield, formerly with Paul Ash. The interviewer says Layfield taught him too and they discuss the Oriental and McVickers theaters.
1050.q: I mean you knew all of the instruments. Me and Mr. Cusick, me and Mr. Roy Knapp, if you say that, let Mr. Roy Knapp say something about it. He was the man from the, what do you call it, the Minneapolis Symphony.

248.t: No real teacher: help from Joe Welch and Manuel Manetta
248.s: Dawson says he taught himself but needed a teacher for note divisions, and got help from Joe Welch and Manetta.
248.q: Yeah, he'd help me. It was the main thing, but, uh, they had another fellow would help me out in that division, too. I don't know if I didn't call his name, Joe Welch.

249.t: Lessons from Lloyd Cantrell and the Imperial method book
249.s: He took lessons from Cantrell using the Imperial method book, and can read anything, including heavy overtures with Pritchett's band.
249.q: Oh, it's got a new method now. My grandkids got the book, I wanted to leave it here by his house he got it. I played with Pritchard Band, them heavy overtures, yeah. I read anything. See, before I was back with the swing, I used to like to read, played them reading all you see. Yeah, you see. After…

917.t: Learning the value of time before an instrument; Bud Scott
917.s: Old teachers required learning time values before touching an instrument. Keppard left the store job and picked up guitar like Bud Scott, whom he praises.
917.q: That's the time you had to pick. You couldn't have no instrument. You had to take and use your feet to hold that time and take and get the value of the time before you get an instrument. Just like you say, one, two, three, four. One, two, three. Wash time, six, eight. Anything but the value of the…

827.t: Little Black Joe and Joe Lindsey, drummers father taught
827.s: Father taught young drummers who worked in his shop and subbed for him: Little Black Joe and Joe Lindsey.
827.q: I can tell you one boy I remember that was a fine little drummer that my daddy taught. He worked for my daddy. And my daddy, we used to call him Joe. Little Black Joe. He was a little dog fella in the car. He worked for my father for years in the shop.

262.t: Learning to read music with Chris Kelly and Port Arthur
262.s: Bailey took lessons in 1921 with Kelly, read music, played on the steamer Capitol, and went to Port Arthur with the Black Eagle band.
262.q: You know when I started trying to take a lesson? 1921 I was playing Chris Kelly. I was learning good. I was reading the music. I was reading. And everybody in the band could read it. See the trammel player from over the river, he used to buy the music and he arranged it. A brother named Harrison…

36.t: Lessons with Tio: counting, keeping time, fingering
36.s: Tio made him keep his foot going to count note values; he demonstrated difficult fingerings on his own clarinet. Simeon also comments on drummers pushing a soloist.
36.q: When I first started, Teo impressed, always impressed it. You had to keep your foot. For whole notes, four beats. For a half note, two beats. A quarter note, one beat. But I always had to keep that foot going while I was playing my exercises. I had to keep the foot going to keep it on time. And…

957.t: Practicing on a cheese box and choice of sticks
957.s: He taught himself on a homemade cheese-box drum with chair-leg sticks and later preferred lightweight Ludwig 2A sticks.
957.q: I always used lightweight sticks. Mm-hmm. Because I could do more with them. I couldn't handle them. Yeah. Yeah.

481.t: Other bands played with and learning drums on tubs, tin pans and boxes
481.s: Bailey lists Chris Kelly, Sam Moore, Buddy Pete, Joe Alva and Jack Carey, says he learned on tubs and tin pans, and describes learning to read drum music.
481.ch: Dave Bailey: recording and learning to play
481.q: When he died. I played Chris Kelly at the time down at... I played him six months during the year. I played a couple of judges with different players.

763.s: The guitar professor trained students to hold tempo by covering the metronome and playing on.
763.q: Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. Well, they could improve. But could you knock it in their head to keep tempo? Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. No. That would be less. That's something that you can't learn a poison. It's got to come from under your heart. Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. In other words, you've got to…

949.t: Lou Dillon the teacher and more modern players
949.s: Suhor credits drummer Lou Dillon as a teacher who shaped Reed and himself and whose methods he used teaching Johnny Vidacovich; more names are listed.
949.q: Rusty Main, who was an incredible player.

286.t: Lessons from Lewis Dumaine: reading drum music and trumpet
286.s: Dumaine taught him to read, drum music and trumpet, and was strict about reading.
286.q: Uh-huh. Yeah. He taught me both trumpet and drums. Uh-huh. Lewis Dumaine and George McCullum. I see. You heard the talking. Yeah. Uh-huh. Well, I went on from there, and when I was playing about, just about four years, I thought of playing with Lewis Dumaine. Lewis Dumaine said, well, don't you…

634.t: Teacher David Jones and wrist technique
634.s: David Jones taught him to read; the rolls he picked up himself, playing from the wrist.
634.q: He didn't teach me no roles or nothing. I just picked that up. But you see some drummers, you know, when they played like this with their whole hand. Now you have them watching me, you never see them seeing my hand move. You see this wrist move. The wrist played direct from the wrist. That's how I…

55.t: Vic Gaspard's lessons: method, scales and snare drum rolls
55.s: The Imperial method, reading treble and bass clef, wrist action, and which New Orleans drummers can make a clean roll.
55.q: everything in the scales I knew the scales I learned the base clip you know I knew the scales on triple click you see I didn't have to worry about no kind of scale I didn't have to transfer to the base clip to the base that's really prepared me a little positive sometime by reading the treble so…

884.t: Joe Howard teaches him to read and to tune a drum
884.s: Joe Howard taught him music from methods and rubber pads, and tuning bass drum to the A string and snare to trumpet.
884.q: On the A string? On the A string? Yeah. On the A string? Yeah. On the A string? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You just know if you got a bass there, just tune up that A string and you just bring that bass up until you bring up that A. And it sounds just like that bass.

885.t: Practicing as a kid and now
885.s: He practiced a lot as a child while playing ball, and still keeps a pad.
885.q: Yeah, very much, very much, very much. I was active. I played ball in all of the games that kids played. I was a catcher on the ball team. So was I. Yeah, and then I, you know, I played all the games. But you have to take time out to play that, to practice that instrument. That's one of the most…

189.s: Davenport credits Professor Tull's down-left-right-up counting method for his timing; the interviewer says his teacher Manetta taught the same.
189.q: Now like this guy, Tull, old Professor Tull, he was a very good music teacher. He was a very good teacher. He took lessons from him too. The old Willie Humphrey. The old Willie Humphrey, yeah. I knew him. He was fine then. And I learned a lot from Alonzo Edson. See, I was teaching up there in…

25.t: Dandy Dixie Minstrels and Professor Wilson
25.s: He joined the Dandy Dixie Minstrels touring Mexico and Texas, took up xylophone and bells, and learned to read from the trumpeter Wilson.
25.q: Well, I went out with it in 19... 1912. And for... and stayed with the... stayed with the sex until it closed. And I joined the Dandy Dixie Minstrels as a drummer for band and orchestra.

303.t: Teaching himself drums and piano; Paul Jacobs
303.s: No lessons on drums or piano; learned chords from books, accompanied singing teacher Paul Jacobs, and learned thousands of tunes by ear.
303.ch: Baton Rouge, marriage, learning to play
303.q: Not one part of them, no. I wouldn't know of, I don't even know the, what do you call it, parabellum or something? Paradiddle. Diddle, paradiddle. I wouldn't know of paradiddle from a monkey doodle, from a Yankee doodle. Yeah.

997.t: What Cottrell taught: snare roll, pad and counting time
997.s: Cottrell stressed snare drum and a good roll, practice on a pad, and beating time with the foot while counting.
997.q: Snare drum, yeah. Good roll, you know. Did you use a drum pad at first? Well, I used a drum pad.

533.t: The Internet, short attention spans and the lost practice habit
533.s: Asked about the Internet, Allen says it makes things too easy; he recalls long practice at school in Green Bay, vanishing school music programs, and Bobby Hutcherson's six-hour days.
533.q: It’s too easy. And you know, I find it even strange to me, hearing myself say that, because I love gadgets. I’m a techie you know. But I think one of the down sides that has come with that is that people in general have a much shorter attention span. You know, the way that we had to get to the…

850.t: Beat-for-beat attention and teaching at Creative Music Studio
850.s: Berger describes his training of giving each beat equal attention so bar lines vanish, and why teaching helped CMS ask what is common to all music.
850.ch: Free jazz, time and the Creative Music Studio
850.q: Yeah, of course, yeah. You have to learn what we call beat-for-beat attention. This is our training that we do with the Creative Music Studio. I call it beat-for-beat attention. That means each beat has the same attention. So you’re not going for like one — and that’s more important than the two or…

315.t: Dan on learning from Alan Dawson after Joe Morello
315.s: Dan says Morello was inspiring but Alan Dawson could explain and taught him a great deal quickly.
315.q: And me as a drummer I was very lucky because Joe was very inspiring you know, it was like oh man I’d love to be able to play like that. But when Alan came along there was someone that could really explain what he was doing. He was just unbelievably brilliant at saying, well tearing things apart and…

1009.t: Staying with Emile Latimer in Buffalo and a dream of drummers
1009.s: Asked about other spiritual paths, he describes living with Emile Latimer, who taught drumming as a way of life, and a dream of drummers he must meet.
1009.ch: Following the drum to New York
1009.q: I am sure. I’m sure there are people who have done it. But for me and for everybody the path is different. Right? For me it really happened in my relationship with the drum. So, and interestingly the drum that I was hearing, which I didn’t know, was batá. And I remember specifically when I went to,…

811.t: Butch Miles as his first drum teacher
811.s: Butch Miles taught him tricks of the trade and technique.
811.q: Okay. I guess he felt my energy. And I wasn’t the most technical, and I never have been really the most technical drummer like a Buddy Rich or Butch Miles, who was my teacher when I was growing up for a year. He was my first drum teacher. It was great. He taught me all kinds of stuff. He goes,…

549.t: Jo Jones and Al Hibbler teach him to listen
549.s: Jo Jones and Hibbler gave him records to identify within a week.
549.ch: Basie alumni and childhood in Hollis
549.q: I’ve never found it again. I’d like to have it. And let’s not leave out Jo Jones, the original, the babysitter, you know I was going to Jo Jones’ apartment learning jazz lessons from Jo Jones, it’s a tough struggle, but I knew him and he was great.

357.t: Drum teacher Tony Spargo and drummer idols
357.s: His first teacher was Tony Spargo of the Original Dixieland Jazz Band; his idols were Wettling, Drootin and Cliff Leeman; Bill Crow's drummer T-shirt joke.
357.q: Yeah. My drummers were — the most primitive one was my drum teacher in 1949 or ’50 I guess, Tony Spargo. He was the drummer with the Original Dixieland Jazz Band.

813.t: Lessons with Jake Hanna fixing his drum technique
813.s: Jake Hanna corrected his grip and technique, and watching him play taught Smith tuning and setup.
813.q: Yes, sure did. Not too early really. I’d been playing quite a while before I took lessons from him. And my early studies were with a pretty generic drum teacher, who said you play a quarter note this way, and do this this way, and do that that way. But despite that he still told me some wrong…

984.t: Joining Nellie Lutcher at twenty and George Clisskins's drum teaching
984.s: He was confident at 20 when joining Lutcher, and credits his teacher George Clisskins and the Stone and Harr books.
984.q: But well I loved her music and it was such a pleasure to play it and I considered myself fortunate to have fallen into this position where I could play with somebody whose music I knew so well and whose music I loved, whose work I loved. And I guess I considered myself pretty fortunate but I think…

1.t: Uncles drumming at home; Cozy Cole's practice pad later
1.s: His four drummer uncles played all day around the house, compared with Cozy Cole practising rudiments in Cab Calloway's dressing room.
1.q: Beating. Yeah, they’d be beating. Paul [Barbarin], he was the oldest. Paul would be beating. He was doing . . . After I joined Cab Calloway’s band, and Cozy Cole would stay in the dressing room all day, practicing ratamacues, flamamadiddles, flama­ ramadiddles, all them kind of drum movements, and…

105.t: Self-taught, with stick-control lessons from Lee Young
105.s: Hamilton says he was largely self-taught, took stick-control lessons from Lee Young, subbed for him, and could not read music but memorized Ellington and Lunceford records.
105.q: Anyway, I started taking lessons from Lee because Lee was playing with Lorenzo Flennoy at the time, the band, with Red Callender, Lee, Red Mack, you know, those guys. Anyway I’m in high school and all of a sudden Lee had me to sub for him every now and then.

471.s: They practiced from books like Slonimsky and records, and the two roommates shared a kit in the kitchen.
471.ch: Cannonball, Miles and the New York scene
471.q: Slonimsky, stick control. Just the books was popular. Coordination books. Just whatever was handy. We would play – read duets. That’s almost like the drum and bugle corps things. We did some of that, and we did a lot of the other stuff.

508.t: Handing Justin Faulkner twenty CDs each from the band
508.s: When Faulkner joined at eighteen the band gave him CDs, from Jo Jones to Shostakovich, and he learned the music in two years.
508.q: But that would have been the guy. I wouldn’t teach him anything. I’d do the same thing I did with him. When he joined the band he was eighteen years old and he had extraordinary ability and didn’t know any music. So I gave him my twenty CDs. Revis gave him his twenty CDs. Joey gave him his twenty…

88.t: Practicing rudiments every morning with Cozy Cole
88.s: He says he learned from every drummer, especially Cozy Cole, a rudimental practice enthusiast who drilled him from the book daily.
88.ch: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
88.q: Now you see, that I don't really know, because I could, you know, being a musician, because I would go to work with Cozy Cole almost every night, and any drummer that could hold the stick I went to hear him play, you know, because I felt as though that I could learn as much from the bad drummers as…

379.t: Chano Pozo at the Spanish Music Center session
379.s: Chano taught Machito's percussionists their parts; Tito Puente learned in his band.
379.q: See, I'm glad you brought that up. That's where Chano Pozo (inaudible) used to try (inaudible). And I'm glad you brought that up because, before Chano got here, Machito Mangual and the whole band Majici used to tell McGuire, Miranda (inaudible) all there, (inaudible) and the conga, that they didn't…

381.t: Cozy Cole's lessons at the Krupa-Cole drum school
381.s: He took lessons for about four months with Cozy Cole at the Gene Krupa and Cozy Cole school on Eighth Avenue and learned rudiments.
381.q: Yes, he is. But Cozy, you know, I took lessons from Cozy, when I was learning how to read, I went to Cozy, when he had a was out of school, because he was on 54th Street and 8th Avenue, and I took lessons from him for about 4 months.
